title: 684029031553/192NV17: 35, Moor Street, Chepstow, NP16 5DE
text:
TRIBIWNLYS PRISIO CYMRU  -  VALUATION TRIBUNAL FOR WALES

Non-Domestic Rating Decision

Page 1 of 5

Appellant: Mrs E G Skov-Newton

Appellant’s Address: 35 Moor Street, Chepstow NP16 5DE

Appeal number: 684029031553/192NV17

The Matter Appealed against: 2017 Rating List

Date of Hearing: Friday 21st September 2018

Appearances: Mr G Overs (for the respondent Valuation Officer)

Date of Decision: 18th October 2018

Decision of Tribunal: Appeal allowed in part

Members of the Tribunal: Mrs E Price-Suter (Chairperson), Mr T Cook, Mr R
Henley

Tribunal Clerk: Mr G Harris

Introduction:

1. Mrs Skov-Newton contended, in a proposal to alter an entry in the 2017
Rating List received by the Valuation Officer on 5th May 2017, that the
Rateable Value (RV) of 35 Moor Street, Chepstow was incorrect and
should be reduced from £10,500 to £7,000 with effect from 1st April 2017.

2. This is a summary of the case and is not intended to be an exhaustive
record of the proceedings. However, the parties can be assured that all
the evidence was fully considered by the tribunal when it arrived at its
decision. Consequently, the absence of reference to any statement, or
evidence, should not be construed as being overlooked.

Summary of the Case

3. Prior to the hearing Mrs Skov-Newton had indicated that she had been
unable to attend and requested that the panel hear and determine the
appeal in her absence. In light of this the clerk presented Mrs Skov-
Newton’s submission to the panel.
4. In her submission Mrs Skov-Newton described how the RV of the appeal
property had increased from £6,600 in the 2010 Rating List to £10,500
upon revaluation for the 2017 Rating List, an increase of £3,900. Mrs

Non-Domestic Rating Decision

Page 2 of 5
Skov-Newton had believed that the RV was based on achievable rent,
which had been confirmed to her in a letter from Mr Overs in which he had
written –
“The rateable value of a non-domestic hereditament none of which
consists of domestic property and none of which is exempt from non-
domestic rating shall be taken to be an amount equal to the rent at which
it is estimated the hereditament might reasonably be expected to let from
year to year.”
Mrs Skov-Newton contended that to expect a rental value of £10,500 for a
shop the size of 35 Moor Street was simply not achievable. She estimated
that a more realistic value would be £6,000/£7,000 in 2018’s retail
environment.
5. Mrs Skov-Newton explained that to be able to justify a rateable value per
m2 you had to know and understand the town and the location of premises
related to footfall and attractiveness and not just look at a street map. Mrs
Skov-Newton referred to St Mary Street which she said was a prime
location and a very attractive pedestrian street that adjoined High Street. It
contained a number of small retail units, cafes and pubs and where the
level of value was £155/£255. She highlighted13 St Mary Street as being
the same size as the appeal property but with a rate of £155/m2, 19 St
Mary Street had the same rate.
6. Mrs Skov-Newton explained that Moor Street had been called by town
councillors the ‘dead end’ of Chepstow, it was located ‘above the Town
Arch’ away from the High Street. Her property, located further from the
town centre, had been valued using £270/m2 whilst properties closer to the
Town Arch/High Street with a larger footfall had a lower value of £230/m2.
Mrs Skov-Newton questioned the correctness of the difference in values.
7. In addition, 4 retail units in Thomas Street, opposite the entrance to Marks
and Spencer some 65m from the appeal property had been valued using
£150/m2.
8. Mrs Skov-Newton stated that since the unfair increase in Business Rates
there had been an alarming closure of retail shops in Chepstow, in the last
2 months there had been 5 closures including the Herbert Lewis
department store which had operated in Chepstow for 170 years.
Independent retailers like her were fighting on all fronts against falling
footfall due to on-line shopping and out-of-town shopping centres and now
unrealistic business rates.
9. Mr Overs, for the Valuation Officer, introduced the appeal property and
described it as being located towards the top end of Moor Street with rear
access to the shop from Thomas Street. He provided the Tribunal with
external photographs, a map of its location and a plan of its layout
together with the Valuation Officer’s survey details. It had been entered
into the 2017 Rating List at a RV of £10,500 with effect from 1st April
2017. He explained that the basis of valuation for the appeal property had

Non-Domestic Rating Decision

Page 3 of 5
been defined under Paragraph 2(1) Schedule 6 of the Local Government
Finance Act 1988 as –
2(1) The rateable value of a non-domestic hereditament [none of which
consists of domestic property and none of which is exempt from non-
domestic rating] shall be take to be an amount equal to the rent at which
it is estimated the hereditament might reasonably be expected to let from
year to year on these three assumptions-
(a) the first assumption is that the tenancy begins on the day by reference
to which the determination is to be made;
(b) the second assumption is that immediately before the tenancy begins
the hereditament is in a state of reasonable repair, but excluding from
this assumption any repairs which a reasonable landlord would
consider uneconomic;
(c) the third assumption is that the tenant undertakes to pay all usual
tenant’s rates and taxes and to bear the cost of the repairs and
insurance and the other expenses (if any) necessary to maintain the
hereditament in a state to command the rent mentioned above.
10. Mr Overs explained that statute further required that the property must be
valued by reference to values pertaining as at 1st April 2015 but having
regard to the physical state of the property and its physical setting as at
the material day, in this case 1st April 2017. Mr Overs valuation of the
appeal property, using a zoning method and a zone A value of £270/m2,
was as follows –

12. Mr Overs explained that the rear access to Thomas Street with Marks and
Spencer and a car park could possibly have generated footfall and hence
a higher zone A value of £270/m2. In light of this Mr Overs requested that
the tribunal confirm a RV of £10,500 in respect of 35 Moor Street.
13. At the conclusion of the hearing, the tribunal decided to reserve its
decision.

The Reasons for Decision

14. Having considered all the evidence placed before it the tribunal decided as
follows: -

15. In her proposal Mrs Skov-Newton had contended that the Rating List was
inaccurate and that the RV of the appeal property should be reduced to
£7,000 with effect from 1st April 2017.

16. In cases such as this the tribunal had to initially consider the rental
evidence available on the appeal property or on comparable properties
within its locality. In the absence of direct rental evidence on the appeal
property as it was owner occupied the tribunal had looked at rents that
transpired on Moor Street as a whole. Considering the weight of evidence,
the tribunal placed less weight on the majority rental evidence provided by
Mr Overs as they had transpired too far away from the AVD of 1st April
2015 and needed to be adjusted accordingly. Similarly, the tribunal placed
little weight on the rent at 5 Moor Street as Mr Overs had stated that it had
been signed between connected parties and the rent at 9 Moor Street,
although effective from 1st August 2015, had been agreed following a rent
review the terms of which had not been specified.

17. The tribunal placed more weight on the passing rent and settlement
evidence at 16B Moor Street with the rent effective from 1st October 2015
and a resulting agreement on appeal of a zone A value of £230/m2.  This
was further supported by Mrs Skov-Newton’s contentions that the zone A

Non-Domestic Rating Decision

Page 5 of 5
rate applied at both St Mary’s Street and Thomas Street was lower than
Moor Street, which had not been disputed by Mr Overs.
18. The tribunal accepted that in valuing properties within a town centre the
usual practice employed by valuers reflected the fact that higher zone A
values applied to properties closer to the city centre thus reflected their
positions as being in a more advantageous trading location. In this case,
the tribunal believed that the location of the appeal property being further
from the city centre warranted a zone A value more on par with that
ascribed to the lower end of Moor Street. Hence £230/m2 was considered
by the tribunal to be a more suitable amount.

19. Taking into account the tribunals decision that the zone A value of
£230/m2 should be applied to the valuation of the appeal property, the
tribunal’s revised valuation was as follows –

£8,900 with effect from 1st April 2017.
